title:
Intelligent
agents
body:
An introduction to artificial intelligence

Intelligent Systems
School of Computer Science · Ciudad Real
Rubén Juárez Cádiz
notes: This unit develops the ability to specify, design and evaluate an agent. The cover is a conceptual AI-generated illustration, not a real system or a plan of the campus. The supplied lecture is the main foundation, with expanded examples and activities. Keep returning to two questions: what information does the agent have, and what criterion determines its action?
ref: UCLM · Computer Science Degree

title: A route towards agent design
body:
01 · FoundationsWhat AI means and how an agent interacts with its environment.
02 · DecisionsRationality, utility, performance measures and constraints.
03 · DesignPEAS, environment properties and agent architectures.
04 · ApplicationsLLM-based agents and the geared Loopover laboratory.

By the end, you should justify what an agent must perceive, remember, decide and learn.
notes: Suggested use: two 80-minute sessions. Session one covers foundations, the vacuum world, rationality and PEAS. Session two covers environments, architectures, LLM-based agents and the laboratory. Extension material can be used for independent study. Controls: arrows or space to navigate, I for the index, N for notes, F for full screen and E for study mode. Simulations work offline. The PDF shows initial examples and exercise answers without running simulations. No answers are stored or transmitted.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title:
The robot arrives.
Was its action good?
body:
It delivers the parcel in 4 minutes.
It crossed a prohibited area.

What else do we need to evaluate its decision?
notes: Opening activity, 2 minutes. Collect responses before explaining. Speed measures only one aspect of performance. We also need the goal, constraints, available information, alternatives and consequences. The campus delivery example is fictional and returns throughout the unit. It does not imply that UCLM operates such a service.
sub: Running example · An autonomous campus delivery
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: Four approaches to artificial intelligence
body:
Human perspectiveRational perspective
ThinkingModel human cognitive processes.Derive conclusions using formal rules.
ActingProduce behaviour comparable to human behaviour.Choose actions that support a goal using the available information.

This course mainly adopts the rational-agent perspective.
notes: The table crosses two questions: do we focus on thought processes or observable behaviour, and do we use people or a normative rationality criterion as the reference? No single cell describes the whole field. Agents may use logic, search or learning. They do not require neural networks. Ask for an example in each cell: a cognitive model, a theorem prover, a conversational system and a planner.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: The Turing Test and its limits
body:
Observable
behaviour

The imitation game compares responses through written conversation.

Conversational test

Language processing, knowledge representation, reasoning and learning.

Total version

Adds perceptual and physical interaction, such as vision and robotics.

Convincing conversation does not certify safety, truthfulness or competence at every task.
notes: Computer vision and robotics belong to the extension called the Total Turing Test, rather than requirements of the basic conversational test. Turing proposed the imitation game in 1950. It is an operational approach to behaviour, not a universal test of consciousness or general intelligence. Ask which evaluation would suit a vacuum robot that cannot hold a conversation.
ref: Supplied material · Turing (1950), Computing Machinery and Intelligence

title: Ideas accumulate
body:
1950

Imitation

Observable behaviour and conversation.

1956

Dartmouth

The field acquires its name.

1980s

Expert systems

Explicit knowledge and rules.

2012

Deep learning

Major progress in visual recognition.

2023

ReAct

Language models interleave reasoning and actions.

Intelligent agents predate LLMs. Search, logic, learning and control continue to work together.
notes: These milestones are a selective overview, not a sequence in which each approach replaces the previous one. Agent-based thinking belongs to classical AI and predates LLMs. ReAct appeared as a preprint in 2022 and as an ICLR paper in 2023. Do not date the origin of intelligent agents to 2025. The 2012 milestone refers to progress in image classification, not the invention of all neural networks.
ref: Supplied material · Yao et al. (ICLR 2023)

title: The basic relationship: agent and environment
body:
Observations · sensors
ENVIRONMENTWhat happens

Campus, people,
doors and obstacles

⇄
AGENTWhat decides

Internal state,
goals and program

Actions · actuators

An observation informs the agent. An action may change the world and future observations.
notes: Interpret this relationship as a causal cycle. Cameras and proximity sensors provide observations to a robot, while motors execute actions. For software, one API can read information and another can modify a system. The same component may play different roles depending on how it is used. The environment includes what the agent program does not directly control.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: Function, program and architecture
body:
f : P* → A

P*: all finite percept histories.
A: the set of possible actions.

The function specifies an action for each history.

FunctionAn abstract description of behaviour.
ProgramAn implementation that computes an action.
ArchitectureThe platform that runs the program and connects inputs and outputs.

Agent = architecture + program
notes: The same vacuum rule can run in a simulator or a physical robot. The agent function describes behaviour, while the program realizes that behaviour. P* includes histories of different lengths. A program can summarize the past in memory rather than store every percept. For randomized behaviour, a more general description returns a probability distribution over actions. Do not confuse agent architecture with neural network architecture.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: State, observation and belief
body:
World state · sₜThe door is closed and someone is behind it.
Observation · oₜThe camera only sees the door.
Belief · bₜSeveral hidden states remain possible.
bₜ(s) = P(sₜ = s | hₜ)

A probabilistic belief summarizes which states are plausible given the history of observations and actions.

Partial observation may require memory or inference.
notes: The history hₜ contains observations and previous actions. A belief may be represented as a set of possibilities or a probability distribution. It is not the same as an LLM verbally claiming confidence. Internal state may also include a map, goals and execution memory. Bayesian filtering algorithms are beyond the scope of this introductory unit.
ref: Supplied material · CS188, Agents · Original teaching example

title: A small world with real decisions
body:
ARobotDirty
B?Dirty
PerceptCurrent location and local dirt status.
ActionsLeft, right, suck and wait.
AssumptionsTwo squares. Accurate sensors. Dirt does not return.
ChallengeClean the world while avoiding unnecessary actions.

The lecturer sees both squares. The agent only senses its current square.
notes: Distinguish the simulator view from the agent input. Two locations and two dirt conditions per square give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 world states. A local percept may be consistent with several world states. Actions are deterministic under these assumptions. This demonstration excludes sensor noise, battery limits and new dirt.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: A perception and memory laboratory
body:
World view for the observer. The agent receives only its local percept.

Available percept
Agent memory
Last action / steps

When can the agent justify choosing “wait”?
notes: Demonstration, 5 minutes. Execute six steps with the reflex agent. It continues moving after both squares are clean. Reset, select memory and repeat. This agent stores known clean, known dirty or unknown for each square. It incorporates local observations and the known deterministic result of sucking. Once both squares are known clean, it waits. This depends on dirt not returning. Changing the policy resets the experiment for a controlled comparison. The PDF shows the initial state, followed by a comparison trace.
ref: Supplied material · Original teaching simulation

title: Memory changes later actions
body:
StepSimple reflexWith memory
1Suck in ASuck in A
2Move to BMove to B
3Suck in BSuck in B
4Move to AWait
5 and 6Keep alternatingWait

If movement consumes energy, the same cleanliness with less movement can improve performance.
notes: Both runs start in A with two dirty squares. After sucking, the memory-based agent incorporates the known effect into its model, so it can wait at step four without revisiting A. A purely reactive policy may be rational if the performance measure does not penalize movement. There is no universally superior program without assumptions and a criterion. Ask what would change if new dirt could appear.
ref: Supplied material · Simulator trace

title: Rationality: deciding with what is available
body:
Choose the action with the best expected performance, given the evidence and the agent’s knowledge.

01CriterionWhat matters
02KnowledgeWhat is known
03OptionsWhat can be done
04HistoryWhat has been observed
notes: Evaluate rationality when the decision is made. Later outcomes do not retroactively change the information that was available. A rational agent is neither omniscient nor infallible. It should also consider useful information that can be acquired at reasonable cost. Connect this definition to the opening example: delivery speed was only part of the task.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: A good decision can still fail
body:
TWO ROUTES · HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE

RouteOutcomeUtility
SafeAlways arrives+6
Fast80% success+10
Fast20% failure−8
EU(fast)
= 0.8 · 10 + 0.2 · (−8)
= 6.4

EU(safe) = 6

The fast route has higher expected utility, although it may fail.

Utilities encode the preferences in this example. They are neither minutes nor percentages.
notes: The model assumes comparable cardinal utilities and known probabilities. With these values, the fast route is better by 0.4 utility units. If failure were ruled out by a mandatory constraint, this utility comparison would not authorize the route. Utility is not synonymous with money. Ask whether one failure proves irrationality. It does not, unless the agent ignored relevant information available at decision time.
ref: Original numerical example · Expected utility

title: When does the decision change?
body:
80%

Success: +10 · Failure: −8
Safe route: +6

Adjust the probability and observe the recommendation.

Fast6.4
Safe6.0

Bar length: EU + 8 on a common scale from 0 to 18. The numbers show expected utility.

The indifference threshold is p = 14/18 ≈ 77.8%.
notes: EU(fast) = 10p − 8(1−p) = 18p−8. Set it equal to 6 to obtain p = 14/18. The slider uses integer percentages, so the visible change occurs between 77% and 78%. Bars are shifted by +8 only to display negative utilities as positive lengths. Do not confuse the display scale with the decision criterion. The simulator compares exact expected values rather than sampling outcomes. The PDF retains p = 0.80.
ref: Original teaching simulation

title: The metric shapes behaviour
body:
Isolated metricPossible unintended behaviourMore complete evaluation
Alerts closedClose alerts without investigation.Confirmed detection, errors and response time.
Tutor messagesProlong the conversation.Learning on a new task and quality of support.
Parcels per hourTake inappropriate shortcuts.Verified deliveries within safety constraints.

External performance, training reward and internal utility can differ.
notes: These are hypothetical design examples, not study findings. Distinguish performance measure, which evaluates a trajectory externally; reward, which supplies a learning signal; and utility, which represents decision preferences. An approximate reward does not guarantee the real objective. Ask for another unwanted consequence and a measurement that would reveal it.
ref: Supplied material · Original examples

title: Preferences and constraints
body:
Preferences with trade-offs

Shorter delivery time.
Lower energy consumption.
Greater comfort.

maximize E[U]

Mandatory conditions

Respect authorized access.
Avoid excluded areas.
Stop if a risk remains unresolved.

a ∈ Aallowed

A high reward does not make a prohibited action permissible.
notes: This is a design extension, not a statement of legal requirements. A finite penalty may be offset by another benefit if everything is combined into one sum. Mandatory conditions may instead require action filtering or an independent control. A software agent should check tool permissions before execution. Safe behaviour also requires recognizing uncertainty and escalating when appropriate.
ref: Teaching extension · Constraints of the fictional scenario

title: PEAS: specifying the task
body:
P

Performance

How is success evaluated?

E

Environment

What world does it operate in?

A

Actuators

What can it change?

S

Sensors

What information does it receive?

PEAS describes the task. An architecture explains how the agent tackles it.
notes: Check that sensors are not goals and actuators are not algorithms. A tutor’s text response is an action. A document collection may belong to the environment, while the retrieval mechanism acts as a sensor. The exact boundary depends on the specification. Performance should be measurable, and priorities or constraints should be clear when it has several dimensions.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: PEAS for the delivery robot
body:
P · PerformanceCorrect delivery, time and energy. Prohibited access is a constraint.
E · EnvironmentBuildings, routes, pedestrians, doors and delivery points.
A · ActuatorsMotors, brake, indicators and delivery notification.
S · SensorsCamera, proximity, localization and battery status.

Scenario assumption: the robot receives an authorized destination and may stop or request help.
notes: This example is constructed for teaching. Distinguish a notification issued by the agent from a message received from a user. Candidate measures include verified delivery rate, median time and energy per delivery. No arbitrary weights are assigned here. Constraints must hold independently of these weights. Ask which sensor or information source would be needed if localization failed indoors.
ref: Original teaching example

title: Activity: a tutor for this course
body:
6 min

In pairs, specify PEAS and suggest a metric that could encourage unwanted behaviour.

Deliverable: four rows and a justification.

One possible answer

PLearning on a new problem and correctness.
EStudent, materials and conversation.
AExplain, give hints and request a check.
SStudent responses, history and documents.

Counting quick answers may reward solving the task without helping the student learn.
notes: Allow two minutes for P and E, two for A and S, and two for discussion. Do not grade by exact wording. Reward measures that reflect learning and distinguish outputs from inputs. The proposed answer can be revealed in HTML and is visible in the PDF. Satisfaction and message count do not alone demonstrate learning. An unaided transfer problem is one possible evaluation.
ref: Supplied material · Expanded classroom activity

title: The environment shapes the design
body:
Before choosing an algorithm,
we need to describe the problem.

Observability · Uncertainty · Temporal dependence
Dynamics · Representation · Other agents · Knowledge
notes: Introduce seven dimensions: the original six plus known versus unknown. These describe the task model, rather than giving absolute labels to a technology. The same system can face different environments. Every classification should state its assumptions and explain a resulting design choice.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: Observing and knowing are different questions
body:
DimensionQuestionDesign implication
ObservabilityCan I observe all relevant state information?Missing information may call for memory or inference.
DeterminismDo the state and action determine the next state?Multiple possible outcomes require uncertainty modelling.
Known / unknownDo I know the transition rules or probabilities?Unknown rules must be estimated or learned.

The next roll of a fair die has an uncertain outcome and a known distribution.
notes: Unknown dynamics and partial observability are different. We can know the laws of a world while being unable to see its state, or see the state without knowing how actions affect it. Determinism refers to a fully specified state and, where relevant, the actions of all agents. Not knowing an opponent’s choice does not imply that the game rules are random.
ref: Supplied material · CS188, Agents

title: Time, representation and other agents
body:
DimensionContrastExample with explicit assumptions
Temporal dependenceEpisodic / sequentialIndependent image labels / route planning.
Change during deliberationStatic / dynamic / semidynamicUntimed puzzle / traffic / timed chess.
RepresentationDiscrete / continuousGrid squares / real-valued position and speed.
InteractionSingle-agent / multi-agentSolo puzzle / a game with an opponent.

Discrete spaces may be finite or countably infinite. A task may mix discrete and continuous variables.
notes: Discrete does not necessarily mean finite. In a semidynamic setting, the relevant world does not change while the agent deliberates, but performance may change with time. In timed chess, the pieces remain fixed during a player’s turn while the clock runs down. Episodic means that a decision does not affect later tasks within the model, not merely that a task has an ending.
ref: Supplied material · Conceptual clarifications

title: Classification depends on assumptions
body:
PropertyClassroom LoopoverTimed chessCampus robot
ObservationFullFull¹Partial
TransitionDeterministicDeterministic²Stochastic in the model
DecisionsSequentialSequentialSequential
During deliberationStatic, no clockSemidynamicDynamic
RepresentationDiscreteDiscrete + clockMixed
Agents / rulesOne / knownSeveral / knownSeveral / partly known

¹ Game state and clock are available. ² The rules determine each move’s effect. The opponent introduces strategic uncertainty.
notes: Use this table to reason rather than memorize labels. In chess, an opponent’s intentions are not part of the formal game state. The clock introduces a time variable. Robot transitions are represented as stochastic because movement and environmental evolution are uncertain. Loopover is static because its board does not change during computation. A timed variant would require revisiting that classification.
ref: Supplied material · Reasoned comparison

title: One changed assumption changes the agent
body: A classification should explain what the agent needs in order to decide.
notes: Change one assumption at a time. Visible puzzle: search over known states. Hidden tiles: maintain possibilities compatible with observations. Noise: consider multiple successors and verify results. Unknown rules: learn the transition model through interaction. These are conceptual variants, not claimed features of the course laboratory. The actual Loopover simulator here retains deterministic rules and full visibility.
ref: Original interactive teaching example

title: Four decision mechanisms
body:
ArchitectureMain informationQuestion answered
Simple reflexCurrent percept and rulesWhich action matches the situation now?
Model-basedMemory and a world modelWhich state explains what I observe?
Goal-basedModel and goal conditionWhich action sequence can reach the goal?
Utility-basedPreferences and consequencesWhich option has the greatest expected value?

Learning can improve any of these architectures. It is not an obligatory final rung.
notes: These conceptual categories may be combined. Goal-based agents usually need a model, and a learned policy may execute reactively. More complexity does not guarantee better performance: a rule may suffice for a simple, well-observed task. Compare computational cost, available information and design guarantees.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: Simple reflex agents
body:
01PerceiveCurrent input
02MatchA rule condition
03ActAssociated action
if dirt == DIRTY:
    return SUCK
if location == A:
    return RIGHT
return LEFT

Strength

Little computation and a fast response.

Limitation

Situations that look the same receive the same response even when their histories differ.
notes: This pseudocode matches the simulator’s reflex policy. It cannot establish that both squares are already clean. If the full world state were observable, a rule over that state could choose to wait. The limitation therefore depends on what counts as the input percept. Ask which two world states can produce the same percept (A, clean).
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: Model-based agents
body:
mₜ = update(mₜ₋₁, aₜ₋₁, oₜ)
Previous memoryWhat had been observed or inferred.
Previous actionWhich change was attempted.
New observationWhich evidence has now arrived.

In the vacuum world

The agent remembers that A is clean while it is in B.

If the world changes

Memory may become stale and require revision.

A model supports state estimation. It does not guarantee that the estimate is correct.
notes: mₜ denotes internal agent state, which need not equal the actual world state sₜ. The update uses transition and perception models. With deterministic, fully known dynamics it may maintain an exact estimate. Noise and hidden information may require a distribution instead. The previous action matters because the agent also changes its environment.
ref: Supplied material · Teaching notation

title: Goal-based agents
body:
Goal

The parcel is at the authorized destination.

Plan

A sequence of actions that reaches that condition.

Replanning

A new observation can invalidate the route.

Search simulates consequences before acting.
notes: The diagram shows modelled possibilities, not movements the robot has already executed. Distinguish a goal state from a particular route. A real action may fail and require observation and replanning. Connect to Unit 2: states, actions, transitions, goal and cost. Search requires a model on which consequences can be simulated.
ref: Adapted from the supplied course material

title: Utility-based agents
body:
Feasible planNormalized time tNormalized energy eU = −(0.7t + 0.3e)
A0.20.8−0.38
B0.50.3−0.44

With these weights

A has greater utility and is preferred.

When energy matters more

With U = −(0.3t + 0.7e), B wins:
−0.36 versus −0.62.

Weights express preferences. Normalization avoids adding incompatible scales.
notes: Synthetic example with t and e between zero and one, where smaller is better. A gives −(0.14+0.24)=−0.38, and B gives −(0.35+0.09)=−0.44. Reversing the weights produces −0.62 for A and −0.36 for B. Inappropriate normalization can distort the interpretation of weights. Both plans are assumed feasible and authorized. Under uncertainty, compare expected utilities.
ref: Original numerical example

title: Learning improves behaviour
body:
PERFORMANCE ELEMENT

Selects actions

Uses the current behaviour.

CriticEvaluates experience against the criterion.
Learning elementUpdates behaviour or its supporting knowledge.
Problem generatorProposes informative experiences.

Exploration can provide useful information, but it also has a cost.
notes: These are functional roles, not necessarily four separate networks. A classifier may learn before deployment and then remain fixed. A reinforcement-learning agent may update through interaction, but we must specify when learning occurs and which changes are allowed. Connect to Unit 6. The performance element selects actions and is not itself the external performance measure.
ref: Supplied material · Sutton and Barto (2018), further context

title: Decision-making also uses resources
body:
A solution that arrives too late may no longer be useful.

Bounded rationality

Time, memory and computational capacity constrain deliberation.

Value of information

More observation is worthwhile when its expected benefit exceeds its cost.

Example: checking a door before planning the entire route may prevent a detour.
notes: This extension introduces two concepts without deriving their algorithms. Bounded rationality recognizes limits on computation. Information has value when it can improve the decision. If a query costs 1 utility unit and increases the optimal expected utility from 5 to 7, its net value is 1. These hypothetical values must use a common scale. Additional data are not useful when they cannot improve a decision or arrive too late.
ref: Teaching extension · Original example

title: The language model within an agent
body:
01ObservationRequest and state
02DecisionSelect a next step
03ToolExecute an action
04ResultVerify and update

The LLM may propose

A query, a response or a structured action.

The system must control

Permissions, arguments, execution, limits and result verification.

ReAct studies the combination of expressed reasoning, actions and new observations.
notes: This extension draws on ReAct without claiming it solves every problem. The approach interleaves reasoning traces and actions in an environment. Generated text alone does not prove that an action occurred. An engineered orchestrator controls tools, interprets results and determines completion. The LLM is one component. In the broad formal sense, the term agent also covers much simpler systems.
ref: Yao et al. (2023), ReAct · Original engineering adaptation

title: Fixed workflow and dynamic selection
body:
AspectPredefined workflowAgent with dynamic selection
Step orderThe design fixes transitions.Depends on runtime observations and decisions.
StrengthPredictable execution of a bounded process.Adaptation when required steps change.
ChallengeExceptions must be modelled.It may select unnecessary or incorrect steps.
Hybrid designMandatory controls and known operations.Limited choice among authorized actions.

Additional autonomy needs a concrete purpose and an evaluation of its outcome.
notes: These are ways of organizing execution, not mutually exclusive classes of intelligence. Fixed workflows may use AI models, and agents may call deterministic subroutines. A predefined workflow may suffice for a task with clear steps. In a hybrid, a model might choose which document to query but be unable to bypass permissions. This is a teaching synthesis, not a normative taxonomy.
ref: Original teaching extension

title: Tool results can also fail
body:
Untrusted inputAn external document may contain instructions unrelated to the task.
Invalid actionMalformed arguments or insufficient permissions may block execution.
Uncertain resultA timeout does not establish whether the action occurred.
Premature completionA convincing answer may hide an unverified objective.

For the tutor: consult a source, check the evidence and acknowledge what cannot be verified.
notes: These are design-risk examples. Possible controls include separating external data from control instructions, checking schemas and permissions, recording execution state and verifying effects before retrying. High-impact actions may require human review. These measures reduce risk but do not constitute a universal guarantee. Useful traces record inputs, actions, results and checks rather than depending on a model’s verbal explanation.
ref: Teaching extension · Hypothetical scenarios

title: Evaluate trajectories as well as answers
body:
What to assessA classroom evaluation approach
Task successVerify the final condition rather than accept a success claim.
ConstraintsCount unauthorized actions or prohibited states.
CostMeasure time, calls and resources under a shared budget.
RobustnessRepeat with varied inputs and controlled failures.
GeneralizationUse held-out cases that were not used to tune the system.

Fair comparisons share tasks, conditions, budgets and evaluation criteria.
notes: Build a small test collection: a normal task, missing data, a failing tool and an ambiguous request. If behaviour is random, run several repetitions and report variation rather than only the best attempt. A simple baseline reveals whether added complexity helps. In the lab, assess valid successors, costs and invalid-argument handling. No experimental results are invented here.
ref: Proposed classroom evaluation

A minus sign means row left followed by column up. The column retains its original index and moves after the row. The lab encodes tiles 00 to 15 in a 32-character string. Exact implementation details should be checked against the supplied lab project, whose code was not attached to this request.

Completed actions: 0

The demonstration splits a legal action into two phases. The intermediate board is not a complete successor.
notes: Start from the ordered board with row 0, column 2 and plus selected. First click: row 0 becomes 03 00 01 02. Second click: column 2 shifts down and the first row becomes 03 00 14 02. Selectors are disabled between phases to keep the action consistent. The mixed example applies three fixed legal actions: 02+, 13− and 31+. Reset restores the goal. This simulator explores transitions rather than calculating an optimal solution. The PDF shows the initial board and the next screen explains the transition.

title: Formulating the search problem
body:
ComponentExample specification
State sA permutation of 00…15, encoded row by row in 32 characters.
Initial state s₀The valid configuration received by the program.
Actions A(s)Row-column pairs and a sign: 4 × 4 × 2 = 32 actions.
Transition T(s,a)Rotate the row, then the specified column.
Goal G(s)s = 00010203040506070809101112131415.
Cost c(s,a)Here, one unit per complete coupled action.

16! ≈ 2.09 × 10¹³ bounds the permutation space. It is not a count of reachable states.
notes: This is a permutation bound, not a claim that all arrangements are reachable under the rules. It explains why unrestricted sequence enumeration is expensive. There are 32 syntactic actions per state, but we do not claim all successors are distinct. Unit action cost is the teaching convention; follow the exact lab specification when implementing. The goal is a predicate rather than a picture.
ref: Laboratory material · Calculations and explicit cost convention

title: Search does not execute every path
body:
State-space graph

Different action sequences may reach the same state.

Search tree

Represents explored paths and may repeat states.

Consequence

Recording visited states can prevent redundant work.

In the laboratory

Correct transitions come before evaluating a search algorithm.

For coupled actions, changing + to − without reversing the order need not undo the action.
notes: Optional extension: the inverse of a composition reverses operation order. A row-then-column move is undone by reversing the column and then the row. The opposite-sign action still applies row then column, so it is generally not the inverse. Validate calculated cases and properties such as preserving all tiles. The original lab image mentions Java, Maven, PicoCLI, bitboards and a verify command, but that code has not been inspected.
ref: Supplied material · Analysis of the transformations

title: Workshop: a cybersecurity agent
body:
An agent reviews access alerts for a university laboratory. It can query logs, request context and propose a response.

10 min

Teams of three.
A one-page design.

1 · SpecifyComplete PEAS and one constraint.
2 · CharacterizeJustify observability, dynamics and other agents.
3 · DesignChoose an architecture and necessary memory.
4 · EvaluateDefine a normal case and a failure case.

Assumption: blocking an account requires authorization. Logs may be incomplete.
notes: Fictional introductory exercise connected to professional practice. Suggested roles: specification, architecture and critical review. The system has no access to real accounts or records. Distinguish proposing an action from executing it. Reward designs that seek more context or abstain when an alert is ambiguous. An LLM is not required. A justified rule-based design with memory is valid.
ref: Original classroom activity

title: A reasoned workshop solution
body:
PEASP: confirmed incidents and false positives. E: accounts and logs. A: query and propose. S: alerts and context.
EnvironmentPartially observable, sequential and dynamic. Other actors may change their behaviour.
DesignPer-alert memory, associated evidence and review status. Rules or utility depending on scope.
EvaluationConfirmed alert, false positive, missing record and unauthorized request.

Suggested rubric: PEAS 3 points · environment 2 · architecture and memory 3 · evaluation 2.
notes: There is no unique solution. Strong answers connect each classification to a design choice: partial observability, for example, motivates maintaining evidence and seeking additional context. More automation requires a clear authorization model and effect verification. An LLM alone does not solve observability, permission or metric problems. The rubric is a proposal, not the official course grading scheme.
ref: Indicative solution and proposed rubric

title: Six questions to check understanding
body:
01

What does P* represent?

All finite percept histories, not just the current percept.
02

Can a rational decision fail?

Yes. It is assessed by expected performance given the available information.
03

Does unknown mean partially observable?

No. Unknown rules and hidden state are different difficulties.
04

Must a goal-based agent learn?

Not necessarily. It may plan with a supplied model.
05

What does utility add to a goal?

It compares the quality of different acceptable outcomes.
06

How many phases does 02+ have?

Two: row 0 right, then column 2 down. Together they count as one action.
notes: Retrieval activity, 4 minutes. Ask students to answer before revealing each explanation. Answers are visible in print. For informal assessment, ask each student to identify the idea that remains least clear. The known-versus-observable item targets a common confusion. For Loopover, the transformation order is part of the answer.
ref: Original learning check

title: Misconceptions we can now correct
body:
Incomplete or incorrect claimCorrection
“Success proves rationality.”Evaluate the choice using information available before the outcome.
“Every agent needs an LLM.”Rules, search and other methods also implement agents.
“Learning means remembering.”Storing information does not necessarily improve a rule or model.
“All discrete spaces are finite.”A discrete set may be countably infinite.
“A goal is enough to compare plans.”A goal tests achievement. Cost or utility compares alternatives.
notes: Ask pairs to select one claim and construct a counterexample. Possibilities include a reflex vacuum agent, exact memory that does not learn, integers as an infinite discrete set, and different-cost routes reaching the same goal. Reward conceptual reasoning rather than sweeping claims about intelligence.
ref: Supplied material · Clarifications and original examples

title: Essential vocabulary
body:
TermMeaning
PerceptAn input received by the agent at a particular instant.
Agent functionA mapping from percept histories to actions.
PolicyA rule for selecting actions from represented information.
Belief stateA representation of possibilities about hidden state.
UtilityA value representing preferences over outcomes.
Transition modelA description of the effects of actions on state.
Goal testA predicate checking whether the objective is satisfied.
notes: Use this glossary to connect the lecture, textbook and lab terminology. Policy and agent function are related, but a policy often takes the state, a belief or a particular information representation as input. Observation and state should only be identified when the model supports full observability.

Formulating problems and searching for action sequences that reach a goal.

notes: Return to the robot that delivered in four minutes after crossing a prohibited area. The observed outcome alone cannot establish performance. A design must specify allowed actions and the information used to decide. Ask for one sentence linking agents and search: a goal-based agent can simulate transitions to choose an action sequence. ReAct is a specific research approach rather than a correctness guarantee.
